replies.author: @johnp.johnson1541
replies.text:
Without landlords, millions more people would be homeless.

Not everyone has $50k cash for a down payment, a 740 credit score, or the desire to lock themselves into a single city for 10 years. Students, military families, mobile professionals, and low-capital workers need a functional rental market.

Furthermore, when a $12k roof fails or a furnace dies, the landlord absorbs that balance-sheet shock. Forcing low-income families into homeownership without capital reserves just guarantees mass foreclosures.

Landlords supply the capital and absorb the risk that makes shelter accessible to people who can't or choose not to buy.

replies.author: @johnp.johnson1541
replies.text:
Treating residential housing as some magical high-return "investment" is a total misunderstanding of capital allocation.

Once you deduct 30 years of property taxes, mortgage interest, insurance, repairs, and agent fees, a primary residence historically yields barely 3% to 4% real annual appreciation. Ask anyone who bought at the peak in rust-belt cities like Buffalo or Scranton decades ago how that "investment" worked out when the local tax base collapsed.

Anyone who actually understands investing would rather plow capital into broad-market index funds like QQQM—which delivered ~20% CAGR since 2009 with zero maintenance, zero property tax drain, and total liquidity.

Homes provide shelter and localized security; they are a terrible substitute for real productive equity compounding.

Real estate investors don't buy "to hoard houses"—they buy cash flow.

Landlording is a yield business based on Net Operating Income after accounting for taxes, insurance, CapEx, maintenance, and vacancy. If a property doesn't cash-flow at current cap rates, serious capital walks away.

Have you ever looked at a real estate balance sheet?

Being a landlord is functionally no different than being a bond holder.

You deploy upfront capital to purchase a yield-generating instrument that pays a regular coupon (net monthly rent) based on the cap rate of the asset. The primary difference is that unlike a paper bond, a lease allows the "coupon" to adjust upward over time with currency debasement.

Treating routine yield-based income allocation as "evil hoarding" just proves you don't understand how fixed-income capital structures or risk-adjusted returns work.

Good luck!

replies.author: @elberethgilthoniel5053
replies.text:
I think you should understand that all the oil offered on the open market can be thought of as one large bucket from which buyers draw their supply. In this sense, a disruption in the supply chain - even one completely unrelated to your own country - can drive up the market value of oil, which in turn leads to price changes for consumers. This is a significant oversimplification, as there are different grades of oil, but taken as a whole, it remains a global market in which domestic consumers are simply one of many competing parties. 

The U.S. faces an additional challenge: it has few oil refineries equipped to process the specific type of crude it produces. The U.S. extracts "light" crude, while its refineries are primarily designed to process "heavy" crude. In effect, the system is balanced in such a way that the U.S. exports its own extracted crude to be refined abroad, while importing finished petroleum products - or purchasing different, "lighter" grades of crude from other countries to process domestically. It’s a rather peculiar imbalance. I agree - it certainly does look kinda strange 👀

comments.text:
An interesting assessment.  I think that you missed a key point for the US, but your analysis pointed me to it:

A homebuyer in the US gets a 30-year fixed mortgage.  You buy the absolute maximum that you can afford, because your mortgage payment will never go up, and even if your salary only goes up with inflation, the payment still becomes a smaller and smaller percentage of your costs/expenses.

If mortgage rates drop, you refinance and enjoy the lower payment.  If rates increase, you don't ever think about refinancing.

The parents (with mortgages from the low interest rate era) are happy.  Their children, who should be enjoying all of the improvements that you note, are being dragged down by the higher mortgage rates - can't buy, buy with higher costs, and/or buy smaller homes to keep their payments affordable.

It will be interesting to see if younger Americans change their opinions if/when rates come down.  Those with high-rate/payment mortgages will see a reduction in mortgage payments (after they refinance their mortgages) or they might choose to buy a bigger/better house and maintain their payment.  Those who are renting because they cannot afford to buy may be able to buy.  And then they'll all be able to enjoy the other improvements that you noted.
